chapter: Europe 1933, New York Cotton Club, Hodges group
title: Being fired by Ellington after Tricky Sam left
summary: He covered Tricky's parts without extra pay, rebelled, was told he was fired, then was called back when no one else knew the parts.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Is it true -- as I've so often heard -- that Duke never fired anybody -- he -- that made a situation such that they would quit -- or do you know of anyone he ever let go?

He fired me at one time. I -- when he lost Tricky Sam. He came to me and wanted'-- I knew Tricky's parts just as close as I could play them. So he came to me and wanted me to play these parts with no extra money. I did it for awhile, and pretty soon I rebelled. So he says 'you're fired.' And without notice -- without union support, or without anything -- I went back to New York that night on the bus. And stayed until they made a trip. I think

it was down around -- let's see -- southern - eastern section. And he had this concert and there was no way he could keep from getting somebody to play Tricky's parts because Tricky was very important in the band.
And nobody knew the parts. I knew them. So here comes the telephone -- come on down here -- everything's for-given. But no money for nothing. So that's they way I -- I went back like something --
Why did you do that?
I thought that everything would be all right.
You thought you would get the money.
Sure. But -- well, I'll read my book. I'll tell him.
By this time -- when was this? Do you remember what year that was?
No, but I know Al Sully was there. So whatever year he was there is one of those.
(inaudible)
Yeah, it could be.
It was in the '40s. Wasn't it after 1940?
I'm pretty sure it was. Yeah. Yup.
Did -- Al [Sully] wasn't terribly popular with the members of the band was he?

I -- he was all right as far as I know except that -- money was so tight in those days that everybody -- you know how you blame the manager for not giving you this and that and everything. It isn't his fault really. I got along very well with Al. Very well, and he was a valuable man in some ways.
I know Duke said he knew how to deal with the kinds of people in the band -- the night clubs --
(Simultaneous conversation)
Yeah.
-- and some of these shooting gallery type characters.
Yeah.
You need Al Sully.
He did. He did. He did very well when he was there.
